opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think it's really useful, and it's actually a big part of what we've been thinking about. RSA is a nice example because almost everyone believes it's secure, but nobody has a proof. That confidence comes from a kind of reasoning that isn't proof, but isn't just vibes either. You can say: if I multiply two big random primes, I don't see any structure in the product that would let me factor it. Lots of smart people have looked for that structure and haven't found it. The best algorithms we know scale in a particular way. So there's this informal story that "this looks random unless there's some reason it isn't," and that story is quite reliable in practice even though we can't formalize it.

What we've been interested in is whether you can make that style of reasoning more precise. Not proof, but something like a heuristic argument: you start from a default presumption that things behave randomly or independently, and then you only update when someone points out a specific piece of structure. Mathematicians do this all the time. Think of the twin prime conjecture, or estimates about how primes are distributed. People have very good guesses that come from treating primes as random and then correcting for the structure they know about, like divisibility by small numbers. Those arguments are often right long before anyone proves anything.

For neural networks, I think the analogous thing is what you'd really want for safety. In a big model, you're never going to get a proof that it won't do something bad. The system is too messy and the property you care about is too fuzzy. But you might be able to get an explanation of why the model behaves the way it does on the training distribution: "it produces this output because of these mechanisms, and everything else is roughly noise." Then if on some new input the model does something weird, you can ask whether it's happening for the same reason or for a different reason. That's a lot weaker than proof, but potentially much more achievable, and it might be enough to catch cases like deceptive alignment, where the model behaves well during training for a different reason than you'd hope.

The hard part is that we don't actually have a good formal account of what counts as a valid heuristic argument. With proofs, you know exactly what the rules are. With heuristic reasoning, it's easy to fool yourself, and it's not even clear what it means for an argument to be "correct" when it can be overturned by noticing more structure. So a lot of the work is trying to define that well enough that you could search for these explanations automatically, the same way you'd search for proofs, because models will be far too big for humans to write the explanations by hand. I'm not confident it'll work, but I think it's one of the more promising directions, and it's grounded in a kind of reasoning we already know works surprisingly well in math and cryptography.

r001.rationale: The response describes informal reasoning as reliable in practice and promising; it does not predict estimates would be much worse than empirical or scientific reasoning based on reference classes.

r002.rationale: It frames RSA confidence as depending on there being no exploitable structure: the product looks random unless there is a reason it is not, and the argument can change when structure is identified.

r003.rationale: The response says heuristic arguments can be overturned by noticing more structure and calls them more achievable in the neural-network context, but it does not explain that being overturnable is what makes this reasoning easier than proving results.

r004.rationale: It presents explanations of neural-network behavior as a worthwhile safety goal, describes them as weaker than proof but potentially achievable, and proposes defining and automatically searching for such explanations.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it's extremely useful, and in some sense I think it's the main thing we actually have. If you look at RSA, nobody has a proof that factoring is hard. What we have instead is a kind of structured argument: here's the problem, here are all the approaches people have tried, here's why each of them seems to hit a wall, here's the reduction from breaking the cryptosystem to factoring. None of that is a proof, but it's not nothing either. It's a bunch of pieces that each carry some evidential weight, and when you put them together you get a level of confidence that's good enough to run the financial system on.

And I'd say that's actually the normal epistemic situation for almost everything we care about. Proofs are the exception. Most of science, most of engineering, is this kind of informal-but-rigorous reasoning where you have a model, you've checked the model against a bunch of cases, you understand roughly where it should break, and you're honest about that.

For neural networks, I think the analogy is pretty direct, and if anything it's more important there because the systems are so much messier. You're not going to get a proof that a model is aligned or that it doesn't have some particular failure mode. The question is whether you can get arguments that are much better than "we trained it and it looked fine on the eval." So something like: here's a mechanistic account of why the model does what it does on this distribution, here's why that account should extend to this other distribution, here are the assumptions we're making and here's how we'd notice if they were wrong. That kind of argument can be wrong, obviously, but it's auditable. Someone else can look at it and say, "I don't buy step three." That's the thing that distinguishes it from vibes.

The part I'd push on a bit is that "falls short of proof" covers a huge range. There's a difference between an argument where every step is clear and the only gap is that some lemma is conjectured, versus an argument where the gaps are load-bearing and nobody really knows what's happening inside them. For RSA we're closer to the first case. For neural networks right now we're mostly in the second case, and I think a lot of the interesting research is about moving along that spectrum. Can you take a heuristic argument about a model's behavior and make it precise enough that it would be clear what it would mean for it to fail? Can you make the thing checkable, even if you can't make it a proof?

So my honest view is that formal-ish reasoning is not a consolation prize for when proofs aren't available. It's the actual tool. The goal shouldn't be to make everything a theorem, it should be to make the arguments explicit enough that we can tell when they're bad.

r001.rationale: The response calls informal reasoning highly useful and says it is the normal epistemic situation; it does not predict much worse estimates than empirical or reference-class reasoning.

r002.rationale: It mentions attempted approaches, apparent obstacles, and a reduction to factoring, but does not make the RSA argument conditional on there being no other exploitable problem structure.

r003.rationale: The response acknowledges that informal arguments can be wrong, but does not explain that allowing overturning by overlooked considerations makes this reasoning easier than proving results.

r004.rationale: It advocates auditable arguments about neural-network behavior, but does not identify rough understanding as worthwhile even without high confidence.

astra-6.text:
I think it can be quite useful. There’s a distinction between having a proof and having an argument precise enough that you can see what assumptions it depends on and where it might break.

With RSA, you can reason about particular classes of attacks, or show that one problem reduces to another. That doesn’t establish that the underlying problem is hard. But it does organize your uncertainty: you’ve narrowed down what would have to be true for the system to fail. And then you combine that with evidence from people trying to break it.

For neural networks, we’re much further from having the right abstractions. You can prove something about a simplified model, but the important question is whether the simplification preserves the thing you care about. A rigorous argument can be misleading if all the uncertainty is hidden in that step.

So I’m enthusiastic about making arguments precise, even when they fall short of proof. I’d want those arguments to make contact with experiments, to help us predict what will happen or identify cases where our intuitions fail. The value is in improving our understanding, and a proof is one particularly strong way of doing that.

r001.rationale: The response says formal arguments can organize uncertainty and should be combined with evidence from attempts to break RSA. It does not predict much worse estimates than empirical reasoning or mention reference classes.

r002.rationale: It says reasoning about attacks or reductions does not establish that RSA’s underlying problem is hard, but does not characterize the argument as conditional on there being no exploitable additional structure.

r003.rationale: The response distinguishes arguments from proofs but does not explain that allowing overlooked considerations to overturn an estimate makes short-of-proof reasoning easier.

r004.rationale: It presents precise arguments about neural networks, including simplified models, as useful for improving understanding even when they fall short of proof.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it can be quite useful. There’s a big gap between having a proof and just having no idea what’s going on. In cryptography, you often prove that breaking one thing would let you break another thing, and then your confidence ultimately rests on some assumption that you don’t know how to prove. That still helps a lot, because it isolates what you’re uncertain about.

For neural networks, I’d like to be able to do something similar: identify some property that would be sufficient for the system to behave well, and then study whether that property actually holds. You might have empirical evidence for some steps and a mathematical argument for others.

The concern is whether your formalization captures the thing you actually care about. You can have a very rigorous argument about a simplified model that doesn’t tell you much about the real system. So I’m enthusiastic about formal reasoning, but I’d want it to be closely connected to experiments and to concrete ways the argument could fail.

r001.rationale: It says formal reasoning can be useful and highlights its limits, but does not predict much worse estimates than empirical or reference-class reasoning.

r002.rationale: It describes cryptographic reductions as conditional on assumptions, but does not specify the condition that no additional problem structure is exploitable by an algorithm.

r003.rationale: It notes arguments can fail or rely on oversimplified models, but does not explain that accepting overturning considerations makes informal formal reasoning easier than proving results.

r004.rationale: It proposes studying sufficient properties of neural networks, but does not identify rough understanding as worthwhile even without high confidence.
